title: Sound: what makes it loud or quiet, high or low
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 5 Physics: How are sounds made? (2.1), Volume and pitch (2.2), Changing the volume of sound (2.3) and Changing the pitch of sound (2.4), plus the speed of sound, hearing ranges, noise and fair-test variables. No textbook needed.
summary: Why does a short string sound higher than a long one, and why does a shout carry further than a whisper? In Class 1 your child found that every sound starts with a vibration. Now they find that sound travels as a push passed from particle to particle, fastest through solids. They learn the two things that describe a sound: volume (how loud, set by the size of the vibration) and pitch (how high or low, set by how fast it vibrates). They run fair tests, build a rubber-band guitar, solve a bottle puzzle, hear the Doppler effect in passing traffic and survey the noise in their street.
builds_on: Class 1: sounds come from vibrations. They travel through air, water, wood and string, and get quieter with distance. Later classes: sound waves, wavelength and frequency in more detail, the ear, and noise pollution and the law.
subconcepts: every sound comes from a vibration
sound is a wave: squashes and stretches (compressions and rarefactions) passed from particle to particle
sound travels through solids, liquids and gases, best through solids
the speed of sound: about 340 metres a second in air
no particles, no sound: the vacuum
volume: loudness depends on the size of the vibration (amplitude)
the decibel scale and safe hearing
pitch: high and low depends on how fast the vibration is (frequency)
frequency in hertz, our hearing range (about 20 to 20,000 Hz), infrasound and ultrasound
the Doppler effect: a moving source sounds higher coming and lower going
strings: shorter, tighter and thinner strings give a higher pitch
air columns: a shorter column of air gives a higher pitch
making sounds louder: sounding boxes, resonance and megaphones
making sounds quieter: muffling and absorbing
fair tests: independent, dependent and control variables
goals: By the end your child can explain how sound travels from a source to the ear, using the idea of particles passing on a push.
By the end your child can explain why sound travels better through solids than gases, and estimate how far away lightning is.
By the end your child can describe volume and pitch, and say what about a vibration changes each one.
By the end your child can change the pitch of a string or a bottle in two ways each, and explain the bottle puzzle.
By the end your child can plan a fair test and name its independent, dependent and control variables.
By the end your child can say what noise does to people and animals, and name a real debate about whether plants respond to sound.
words: the tiny bits that everything (solids, liquids and gases) is made of
a space with no particles in it, not even air
how loud or quiet a sound is
how big a vibration is: how far it moves back and forth
the unit for measuring how loud a sound is
how high or low a sound is
how many vibrations happen in one second
the unit of frequency: one vibration a second
sound too high for people to hear
sound too low for people to hear
when one thing makes another vibrate strongly along with it
the one thing you change on purpose in a test

the change in pitch you hear when a sound source moves towards or away from you

days.title: How sound travels
days.goal: Recall that sound is vibration, and discover how it travels.

steps.title: What do you remember?
steps.do: Ask: 'In Class 1 you made rice dance on a drum and built a string telephone. What did they show?' Good answers: every sound comes from a vibration. Sound travels through air, string and wood. Sounds get quieter further away. Then your child puts their fingers on their throat and sings a high note, then a low note. Ask: 'Does the buzz feel different?' Let them describe it. Say: 'This time we'll find out what makes a sound high or low, loud or quiet, and how it travels.'

steps.title: Story: The Bottle That Was Too Low
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain the puzzle in it: your child will solve it on Day 5. Ask: 'Parvathi said take water out. Malar added water. Why were they both right?' Write your child's guess on a slip and keep it.

steps.title: The spoon bell
steps.do: Do experiment e1. Tie a steel spoon to the middle of a 1-metre string. Your child wraps the string ends round their index fingers and swings the spoon gently against a table edge. Ask: 'If you press your fingers to your ears, will it sound different? Why?' Then they press their fingertips, with the string, gently against the openings of their ears, and swing it again. Ask: 'Why was it so much louder the second time?' Good answer: the vibration travelled up the string to the ears, instead of spreading out through the air.

steps.title: The pass-it-on line
steps.do: Show how sound travels. Stand three or four family members in a line, shoulders nearly touching. Gently push the first person. Each one passes the push on to the next, then sways back to their place. Ask: 'Did anyone walk from the start to the end? What travelled?' Good answer: only the push travelled. Each person stayed in place. Say: 'Everything is made of particles, far too small to see. A vibrating thing pushes the air particles next to it, and they push the next ones. Sound is this push, passed along. In a solid, the particles are packed tightly, so the push passes on fast. In a gas like air, they are far apart. In a vacuum there are no particles at all, so sound cannot travel.' Draw dots close together for a solid, a little apart for a liquid, and far apart for a gas.

days.title: Through solids, liquids and gases
days.goal: Run a fair test on which materials carry sound, and find how fast sound travels.

steps.title: Fair test: what carries sound best?
steps.do: Do experiment e2. First plan it with your child. Ask three questions and write down the answers. 'What will we change?' The material: air, wood, water or string. This is the independent variable. 'What will we measure?' How loud the tap sounds, on a scale of 0 to 5 or with a sound-meter app. This is the dependent variable. 'What must we keep the same?' The same coin, the same tap, the same distance and the same listener. These are the control variables. Then run the test and record the scores in a table.

steps.title: How fast is sound?
steps.do: Say: 'In air, sound travels about 340 metres every second. That is about three football fields in one second. Light is almost a million times faster.' Ask: 'Why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?' Good answer: the light reaches us almost at once, but the sound takes longer. Teach the rule: count the seconds from the flash to the thunder, then divide by 3. That gives roughly how many kilometres away the storm is. Ask: 'If you count 9 seconds, how far away is the storm?' Good answer: about 3 kilometres. Add: 'In water, sound travels about four times faster than in air. In steel, it is about fifteen times faster.'

steps.title: How bats find their way in the dark
steps.do: Tell the story of voice v1. In the 1790s, Lazzaro Spallanzani found that bats who could not see still flew safely in the dark. Louis Jurine plugged bats' ears, and they crashed. About 140 years later, Donald Griffin used a special microphone and finally recorded their ultrasound calls. Ask: 'Most scientists laughed at Spallanzani. What evidence did he have? What was missing?' Good answer: he showed that bats need their ears, but nobody could detect the sounds. Ask the voice question. Then ask: 'Spallanzani blinded bats, and that hurt them. Is it fair to harm an animal to find something out? Could he have found out another way?'

need: a wooden table or a long wooden plank
a 3-metre string and two paper cups
a phone with a free sound-meter app if you have one

days.title: Loud and quiet: volume
days.goal: Find that a bigger vibration makes a louder sound, and measure volume in decibels.

steps.title: Bigger shake, louder sound
steps.do: Do experiment e3. Use the cling-film drum with a pinch of rice. Tap gently, then harder, then hardest. Your child watches how high the rice jumps and says how loud it sounds. Then pluck a rubber band gently, then pull it further and let go. Ask: 'What changes when the sound is louder?' Good answer: the drum skin or band moves further back and forth. Say: 'How far a vibration moves is called its amplitude. Bigger amplitude, louder sound. The pitch doesn't change, only the volume.'

steps.title: Decibel detectives
steps.do: Do activity a1. Use a free sound-meter app, or without one, a 0 to 5 loudness scale by ear. Measure a whisper, normal talking, the mixer grinder, the television at your usual volume, the road outside and a pressure cooker whistle. Record each in a table. Say: 'Decibels do not go up like an ordinary count. Every 10 decibels more means about ten times more sound energy. So a pressure cooker whistle carries far more than twice the energy of talking.'

steps.title: How loud is too loud?
steps.do: Show this ladder of loudness. Rustling leaves are about 20 dB. A whisper is about 30. Talking is about 60. Busy traffic is about 80. Many hours above 85 can slowly damage hearing. A wedding speaker up close is 100 to 110. A big cracker close by can reach 140, which can harm the ear at once. Ask: 'Which of the sounds we measured were above 85?' Say: 'Hearing lost from loud noise does not come back. The tiny hair cells in the inner ear that sense sound do not grow back.' Ask: 'What could a family do to protect their ears?' Good answers: turn the volume down, keep away from speakers, cover the ears, use earplugs.

steps.title: Volume and distance
steps.do: Ask: 'In Class 1 the sound got quieter as you walked away. Is that because the vibration changed, or because the push spread out?' Good answer: the push spreads out in all directions, so less of it reaches your ear. Draw a dot with circles spreading out, like ripples in a pond. Ask: 'Why do people cup their hands round their mouth to shout?' Good answer: it sends more of the sound one way instead of spreading it everywhere.

need: a phone with a free sound-meter app (optional)

days.title: High and low: pitch
days.goal: Find that faster vibrations make higher sounds, and meet hearing ranges and Raman's drums.

steps.title: The ruler twang
steps.do: Do experiment e4. Hold a plastic or wooden ruler flat on a table with 25 cm hanging over the edge. Twang the free end. Then try 20, 15 and 10 cm. Your child records whether the pitch goes up or down and watches how fast the ruler moves. Ask: 'When the ruler is short, does it shake faster or slower?' Good answer: faster. Say: 'How many times something vibrates each second is its frequency, measured in hertz. Faster vibration, higher frequency, higher pitch.'

steps.title: What we can and cannot hear
steps.do: Say: 'Young people hear from about 20 vibrations a second (very low) to about 20,000 a second (very high). Below that is infrasound: elephants, whales and earthquakes make it. Above that is ultrasound: bats, dolphins and some insects use it. Dogs hear up to about 45,000 hertz.' Ask: 'Why might a dog whistle be silent to you but not to the dog?' Add: 'As people get older, they usually lose the highest sounds first.' If you have a phone, play a 'hearing range test' sound from about 8,000 to 17,000 hertz at LOW volume and see who in the family stops hearing it first.

steps.title: Raman and the tabla
steps.do: Show a tabla or mridangam if you have one, or a picture. Point at the black patch on the skin. On a tabla it is called the syahi. Tell your child about voice v2: C.V. Raman showed that this black patch is why these Indian drums give a clear musical note, which most drums cannot. Ask the voice question. Then ask: 'Who knew how to make the black patch long before Raman studied it?' Good answer: generations of drum makers, who learned by ear and hand and passed it on.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. Your child does it alone, and you read out any item they ask about. Then check the answers together and talk about any mistakes.

need: a tabla, mridangam or picture of one

days.title: Changing pitch: strings and air
days.goal: Change the pitch of strings in three ways, and solve the bottle puzzle from the story.

steps.title: Rubber-band box guitar
steps.do: Do activity a2. Stretch rubber bands of different thicknesses over an open shoebox or tiffin, with a pencil underneath as a bridge. Test one thing at a time. First, a thick band against a thin band at the same tightness. Next, the same band stretched tighter. Last, the same band with a finger pressing it shorter. After each test, your child writes the rule: shorter, tighter or thinner gives a higher pitch. Ask: 'How does a veena or sitar player change the note?' Good answer: pressing the string against a fret makes it shorter, and turning the peg makes it tighter.

steps.title: The bottle jal tarang puzzle
steps.do: Do experiment e5. Put different amounts of water in four identical glass bottles. Ask: 'When you tap, which will be highest? When you blow?' First, tap each bottle gently with a steel spoon and put them in order from low to high. Then blow across the top of each and order them again. Ask: 'What happened? Is it the same order?' Good answer: the order is the opposite. Now go back to your child's guess about the story, written on Day 1.

steps.title: Why opposite?
steps.do: Ask: 'When you tap, what vibrates?' Good answer: the glass and the water in it. Say: 'More water makes it heavier, so it vibrates more slowly and the pitch is lower.' Ask: 'When you blow, what vibrates?' Good answer: the column of air above the water. Say: 'More water leaves a shorter column of air, which vibrates faster, so the pitch is higher.' Ask: 'So were Parvathi and Malar both right?' Good answer: yes, because Parvathi's bowls are struck and Malar's bottles are blown. Ask: 'In a flute, how do the holes change the pitch?' Good answer: opening a hole makes the vibrating column of air shorter, so the note goes higher.

days.title: Louder and quieter: amplifying and muffling
days.goal: Test which materials muffle sound, see how instruments amplify, and hear whale songs change.

steps.title: Fair test: the best muffler
steps.do: Do experiment e6. Put a phone alarm in a small box. Wrap the box in one material at a time: nothing, a cotton towel, newspaper, aluminium foil, a woollen sweater and bubble wrap. Your child measures the loudness from the same spot each time, with the sound-meter app or by counting steps away until they can't hear it. Before starting, your child writes down the independent, dependent and control variables and guesses which material will muffle best. Ask: 'Which materials muffled best? What do they have in common?' Good answer: thick, soft materials with lots of trapped air soak up sound best.

steps.title: How instruments get louder
steps.do: Pluck a rubber band stretched between two fingers in the air: very quiet. Now stretch it over the open box: much louder. Ask: 'Why?' Say: 'The band makes the box and the air inside it vibrate too. This is called resonance. The big hollow body of a veena, guitar or tanpura is a sounding box that makes the string's sound louder.' Roll paper into a megaphone and talk through it. Ask: 'Why does a megaphone make your voice louder in one direction?' (It stops the sound spreading out everywhere.)

steps.title: Songs that change
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v3. Frank Watlington, an engineer, first recorded humpback whale songs. Katy Payne later found that all the whales in an area slowly change their song together, year by year. If you can, play a short recording of humpback song from a museum or nature website. Ask: 'Deep in the sea it is dark. Why is sound more useful than light for whales?' Good answer: sunlight fades within a few hundred metres of seawater, but low sounds can travel hundreds of kilometres. Then ask the voice question.

need: a cotton towel, newspaper, foil, a woollen sweater and bubble wrap
paper and tape for a megaphone

days.title: Sound waves, the Doppler effect and resonance
days.goal: See sound as a wave of squashes and stretches, hear the Doppler effect, and feel resonance in your own body.

steps.title: The compression dance
steps.do: Hold a slinky stretched between you and your child, or lay it on a smooth floor. Slinkies are sold cheaply in toy shops. Give one end a sharp push forward. Watch a bunched-up part travel along it. Say: 'The squashed part is called a compression. The stretched part behind it is called a rarefaction. Sound in air works the same way: squash, stretch, squash, stretch, passed from particle to particle. The distance from one squash to the next is the wavelength. High notes have short wavelengths, and low notes have long ones.' Then do it with people. Family members stand in a line, an arm apart. Clap a slow beat. On each clap, the first person steps forward and back, and each person copies the one before them a moment later. Ask: 'Where are the squashes now? Did anyone travel to the end?'

steps.title: The Doppler effect
steps.do: Stand on a footpath, well back from the road, with a grown-up holding your hand. Listen to motorbikes, autos and buses that honk as they pass. If a railway line is near, listen to a train horn from a platform. Ask: 'Does the sound change as it goes past you?' Good answer: it is higher as it comes towards you, then drops lower as it goes away. Back home, draw circles to explain. Say: 'A moving source squashes its sound waves together in front of it. Shorter waves give a higher pitch. Behind it, the waves are stretched out, so the pitch is lower. The horn itself does not change. Only what you hear changes. This is called the Doppler effect, after Christian Doppler, who described it in 1842. Astronomers use the same idea with light to tell whether a star is moving towards us or away.'

steps.title: Om in the bathroom
steps.do: Chant one long, low 'Om' (aaa-ooo-mmm) together, first in an open room, then in the bathroom with the door shut. Put one hand flat on your chest and the other on top of your head. Ask: 'Where is it louder and fuller? Where do you feel it in your body?' Good answers: louder in the bathroom. The chest buzzes on 'aaa' and 'ooo', and the lips and head buzz on 'mmm'. Say: 'Your chest, throat, mouth and nose have hollow spaces that resonate, like the hollow body of a veena. In the bathroom, the hard tiles reflect the sound back, so it builds up.' Then, in the bathroom, hum one steady note and slide it slowly from low to high. Ask: 'Did the room boom more at some notes than others?' Say: 'Those are the notes the room itself resonates with.'

steps.title: Draw the wave
steps.do: Your child draws three pictures of sound as lines packed close (compressions) and far apart (rarefactions): a low drum (lines far apart), a high whistle (lines close together), and an ambulance driving past a child (lines squashed in front, stretched behind). Label one wavelength on each. Ask: 'Which drawing shows a sound that is loud? How could you show loudness in a drawing?' (Darker, thicker lines for bigger squashes: bigger amplitude.)

need: a slinky, or family members for the line
a grown-up to stand with you near a road, safely back from traffic

prep.task: Find a safe spot on a footpath or bridge to listen to passing traffic or trains

days.title: Noise in my community
days.goal: Survey the noise around home, think about who it harms, and weigh a debate about listening plants.

steps.title: Project: noise survey
steps.do: Start the project. With a grown-up, measure the sound level for one minute at four places: inside your home, at the gate, beside the main road, and in the quietest place you can find (a park, a temple courtyard, a terrace). Use the sound-meter app or the 0 to 5 scale. Record the time and what made the sound (horns, construction, birds). Ask: 'Who lives or works in the loudest place all day?' Good answers: traffic police, street vendors, guards, birds and street dogs.

steps.title: Do flowers listen?
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v4: evening primrose flowers made sweeter nectar within minutes of hearing the hum of a bee. Ask: 'What would you need to see before you believed it?' Good answers: other scientists repeating the test, a control where the flowers hear a different sound, and checks that it isn't heat or a smell. Then ask the voice question. Say honestly: 'Scientists are still arguing about this. It's an open question.'

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 alone. Afterwards, ask your child to read out their answers to the two written items, and ask one follow-up question for each: 'How do you know?'

need: a phone with a sound-meter app (optional)

days.title: Check, challenge and teach it back
days.goal: Play the pitch-and-volume game, tackle the challenge sheet and teach the family.

steps.title: Higher or Louder? card game
steps.do: Play the card game g1. Read the rules aloud first. When a player gets one wrong, they must test it if possible (with the ruler, rubber bands or bottles) before the next turn.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3. Encourage your child to draw diagrams for the written items. Afterwards, talk about the Pythagoras item together and read the Pythagoras challenge.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child gives a 5-minute 'sound show' for the family: the spoon bell, the ruler twang, the bottle puzzle and the noise survey results. They must use the words vibration, particles, volume, amplitude, pitch and frequency. Then ask the check questions. Finish with: 'What is one thing about sound that nobody knows yet?'

need: the ruler, rubber-band guitar and bottles

experiments.title: The spoon bell
experiments.question: Does sound travel better through string than through air?
steps: Tie the spoon to the middle of the string.
Wrap the string ends round your index fingers and let the spoon hang.
Swing it gently against a table edge and listen.
Now press your fingertips gently against the openings of your ears (not inside) and swing it again.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the spoon sound different when the string touches your ears?'
experiments.observe: Through the string, the spoon sounds loud and deep, like a temple bell. Through the air it is a thin, quiet clink.
experiments.why: The spoon's vibration travels up the string and through your fingers to your ears. In the string the particles are packed close, so they pass the vibration on with little loss. Through the air, most of the vibration spreads out in every direction.
experiments.safety: Swing the spoon gently and keep it away from faces.

experiments.title: Fair test: what carries sound best?
experiments.question: Does sound travel better through solids, liquids or gases?
need: a balloon filled with water and tied
a string telephone (two cups, 3 metres of string)
a sound-meter app, or a 0 to 5 loudness scale
steps: Agree the variables and write them down. Independent: the material. Dependent: how loud the tap sounds. Control: the same coin, the same tap strength, the same distance of 1 metre, and the same listener and ear.
Air: your child listens 1 metre from where you tap the coin on a wooden block or a book.
Wood: your child puts their ear on the table 1 metre from where you tap the table.
Water: your child holds the water balloon against their ear while you tap the far side of the balloon with the coin at the same strength.
String: your child listens through the tight string telephone while you tap your cup.
Repeat each test three times and record the scores in a table.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to rank the four before testing.
experiments.observe: Wood and water usually sound much louder than air. The tight string is loud too. Repeating each test shows whether the results are reliable.
experiments.why: In solids and liquids the particles are much closer together than in a gas, so they pass on the vibration more easily and with less loss. Sound also travels faster in them: about 340 metres a second in air, about 1,500 metres a second in water, and several thousand metres a second in wood or steel.
experiments.safety: Tap gently. Nothing goes inside the ear.

experiments.title: Bigger shake, louder sound
experiments.question: What changes about a vibration when a sound gets louder?
need: a steel bowl with cling film stretched tight
steps: Put the rice on the cling-film drum.
Tap gently, then harder, then hardest. Watch how high the rice jumps.
Stretch a rubber band over a box and pluck it gently, then pull it further before letting go.
Listen to both the loudness and the pitch each time.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'If we hit harder, will the sound be louder, higher, or both?'
experiments.observe: Harder taps make the rice jump higher and the sound louder. The pitch stays about the same.
experiments.why: Hitting harder makes the drum skin move further back and forth: a bigger amplitude. That pushes the air particles harder, so more energy reaches your ear and the sound is louder. How fast it vibrates (and so the pitch) depends on the drum, not on how hard you hit it.

experiments.title: The ruler twang
experiments.question: How does the length of a vibrating object change its pitch?
steps: Hold the ruler firmly flat on the table edge with 25 cm hanging over.
Push the free end down and let go. Listen and watch.
Repeat with 20 cm, 15 cm, 10 cm and 5 cm over the edge.
Record: pitch (higher or lower than the last) and how fast the end moved.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will a shorter ruler sound higher or lower?'
experiments.observe: The shorter the free part, the faster it vibrates (it becomes a blur) and the higher the pitch. A very long overhang wobbles slowly and you may not hear a note at all.
experiments.why: A shorter, stiffer piece springs back more quickly, so it vibrates more times each second: a higher frequency. Our ears hear a higher frequency as a higher pitch. Very slow wobbles (below about 20 a second) are too low for us to hear at all.
experiments.safety: Hold the ruler firmly so it doesn't fly up. Keep faces back.

experiments.title: The bottle jal tarang puzzle
experiments.question: Does adding water make a bottle's note higher or lower?
need: 4 identical glass bottles (empty sauce or squash bottles work)
steps: Put a little water in bottle 1, a quarter in bottle 2, half in bottle 3 and three-quarters in bottle 4.
Tap each bottle gently on the side with the spoon. Put them in order from lowest to highest note.
Now blow gently across the top of each bottle until it hoots. Put them in order again.
Add or pour out water to tune the blown bottles to a simple tune, such as the first notes of 'Sa Re Ga Ma'.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which bottle will have the highest note when you tap? When you blow?'
experiments.observe: When tapped, the fullest bottle is lowest. When blown, the fullest bottle is highest. The orders are opposite.
experiments.why: Different things vibrate. Tapping makes the glass and water vibrate: more water means more mass to move, so slower vibrations and a lower pitch. Blowing makes the column of air above the water vibrate: more water leaves a shorter air column, which vibrates faster and gives a higher pitch, just as in a flute or a bansuri.
experiments.safety: Tap gently so the glass doesn't crack. A grown-up clears up any broken glass.

experiments.title: Fair test: the best muffler
experiments.question: Which material is best at muffling sound?
need: a cotton towel, newspaper, aluminium foil, a woollen sweater, bubble wrap
a sound-meter app or a measuring tape
steps: Write the variables: independent (the wrapping material), dependent (loudness, in dB, from 1 metre away, or the number of steps away before you can't hear it), control (same phone, same alarm, same volume, same box, same distance, same amount of material).
Measure the alarm in the open box first, with nothing round it.
Wrap the box in each material in turn, using two layers each time, and measure again.
Repeat each one twice and record in a table.
Rank the materials from best to worst muffler.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to rank the materials before testing.
experiments.observe: Thick, soft, fluffy materials such as the sweater and towel muffle best. Foil and newspaper muffle less.
experiments.why: Soft, fluffy materials are full of tiny pockets of air and loose fibres. When sound hits them, the vibration makes the fibres rub and bend, which turns the sound energy into a tiny amount of heat instead of passing it on. Hard, smooth surfaces reflect sound instead, which is why empty rooms echo.

activities.title: Decibel detectives and the noise survey
need: a phone with a free sound-meter app, or a 0–5 loudness scale
steps: Make a table: sound, place, time, loudness (dB or 0–5).
At home, measure a whisper, talking, the mixer, the TV and a pressure cooker whistle.
On Day 8, use the same table outdoors: inside the home, at the gate, beside the main road and in a quiet place.
Mark every reading above 85 dB in red.
Draw a bar chart of the outdoor readings.
activities.outcome: A table and bar chart of real noise levels, and a list of who is exposed to the loudest ones.

activities.title: Rubber-band box guitar
steps: Stretch the rubber bands across the open box, thinnest to thickest.
Slide a pencil under them near one end as a bridge.
Pluck each band. Which is highest?
Pull one band tighter by wrapping it round the box once more. Pluck again.
Press one band down on the pencil with a finger at different places to make it shorter. Pluck.
Write three rules for pitch: length, tightness and thickness.
activities.outcome: A playable guitar and three tested rules for changing pitch.

voices.who: Lazzaro Spallanzani (1729–1799), Italy, Louis Jurine (1751–1819), Switzerland, and Donald Griffin (1915–2003), USA
voices.idea: In the 1790s Spallanzani blinded bats and found that they still flew through a room strung with threads without hitting them. Jurine, a surgeon in Geneva, then plugged bats' ears, and they crashed. Spallanzani repeated this and concluded that bats find their way with their ears.
voices.then: Most scientists mocked the idea, because no one could hear bats making any sound. The famous naturalist Georges Cuvier argued that bats used a fine sense of touch in their wings. For almost 140 years the 'ear' idea was largely ignored.
voices.now: In 1938 Donald Griffin used a special microphone built by the physicist G.W. Pierce and detected the bats' ultrasound calls. With Robert Galambos, he then proved that bats find their way by echoes. He named this echolocation. Spallanzani and Jurine were right. They just had no way to detect the sound.
voices.ask: Spallanzani had strong evidence but no one could hear the sounds. Should scientists believe a result before they understand how it works? What would have convinced you?

voices.idea: Raman, who later won the Nobel Prize for his work on light, also studied the physics of musical instruments. In papers from 1920 onwards he showed that the tabla and mridangam are unusual: most drums give a muddle of unrelated vibrations, but the black loaded patch (syahi) in the centre of the skin tunes the vibrations so that they ring together like a musical note with harmonics.
voices.then: Physicists knew that an ordinary drum skin vibrates in many ways that do not fit together into one clear note. Raman showed with careful experiments that Indian drum makers had solved this hard problem.
voices.now: It is accepted, and scientists still use mathematics and computers to study exactly how the syahi works. The drum makers who developed the syahi over centuries, mostly unnamed craftspeople, never wrote it down as physics but knew it by ear and hand.
voices.ask: The drum makers knew how to make the syahi, and Raman explained why it works. Which is the bigger discovery? Can you discover something without writing it down?

voices.who: Katy Payne (born 1937) and Roger Payne (1935–2023), USA, and Frank Watlington
voices.idea: In the 1950s and 60s Frank Watlington, an engineer working on underwater microphones for the US Navy off Bermuda, recorded strange long sounds from humpback whales and shared them with the Paynes. Roger Payne and Scott McVay showed in 1971 that the sounds were songs, with themes that repeat. Katy Payne discovered that the songs slowly change, and all the whales in an area change their song together, year after year.
voices.then: Many scientists doubted that animals other than birds and people could have changing songs that are passed on. The recordings, released as an album in 1970, became famous and helped the campaign to stop the hunting of whales.
voices.now: It is accepted. Later research has found that new songs can spread from one ocean population to another over a few years, like a fashion. Why the whales sing and why the songs change is still debated.
voices.ask: The whale songs were first recorded by someone who was looking for submarines. How often do you think big discoveries come from people who were looking for something else?

voices.who: Lilach Hadany and colleagues, Tel Aviv University, Israel (published 2019)
voices.idea: Marine Veits, Lilach Hadany and colleagues played the sound of a flying bee to beach evening primrose flowers. Within about three minutes the flowers' nectar became sweeter, while flowers played silence or high-pitched sounds did not change. The bowl-shaped petals vibrated at the bee's frequency, like an ear.
voices.then: Some scientists were excited: plants might 'hear' their pollinators. Others asked for the test to be repeated by other teams, with more flowers and more careful controls.
voices.now: It is debated. The result is intriguing but has not yet been widely repeated, and nobody knows how many plants might respond to sound, or how.
voices.ask: One study found an exciting result. What would you need to see before you believed that flowers can hear bees?

project.title: Noise in my community
steps: On Day 3, measure sounds at home and learn the decibel ladder.
On Day 8, with a grown-up, measure for one minute in four places: inside your home, at the gate, beside the main road and in the quietest place you can find.
Record what made the sound in each place and the time of day.
Make a bar chart and mark readings above 85 dB in red.
Write three sentences: Who is exposed to the loudest noise, and for how long? Which animals live there? What is one change that would make the loudest place quieter?
Share your chart with a neighbour, your residents' association or your school.
project.outcome: A noise chart of your neighbourhood, a list of who and what it affects, and one suggestion for making it quieter.

game.title: Higher or Louder?
rules: Cut out the question cards and shuffle them face down. Put the four category cards face up.
On your turn, take the top card and read the front aloud.
Say your answer and which category it belongs to: PITCH, VOLUME, TRAVEL or HEARING.
Turn the card over. If you are right, keep it. If you are wrong, put it at the bottom of the pile, and test it with the ruler, bands or bottles if you can.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins.

cards.front: PITCH
VOLUME
TRAVEL
HEARING
You make a guitar string shorter. Higher or lower?
You loosen a veena string. Higher or lower?
Thick rubber band or thin one: which is higher?
You blow across a bottle that is nearly full. High or low?
You tap a bottle that is nearly full. High or low?
A long flute or a short flute: which plays lower?
You hit a drum harder. What changes?
cards.back: Volume goes up, because the amplitude is bigger (VOLUME)

cards.front: Roughly how loud is normal talking?
Above about how many dB, for many hours, can noise damage hearing?
Why does a veena have a big hollow body?
Woollen sweater or steel plate: which muffles better?
Does sound travel fastest in air, water or steel?
Can sound travel through a vacuum?
cards.back: No: no particles to pass it on (TRAVEL)

cards.front: Thunder comes 9 seconds after lightning. How far away?
How fast is sound in air, roughly?
Why does sound get quieter far away?
cards.back: It spreads out in all directions (TRAVEL)

cards.front: Can young people hear 30,000 hertz?
What do bats use to find moths?
What is sound too low for us to hear called?
Who usually loses the highest sounds first: children or grandparents?
Which animals sing songs that change every year?
Which flowers may make sweeter nectar when they hear a bee?
An ambulance drives towards you, then away. What happens to the siren's pitch?
cards.back: Higher coming, lower going: the Doppler effect (PITCH)

cards.front: Why do people sound better singing in a tiled bathroom?
cards.back: Hard walls reflect the sound and it resonates (VOLUME)

big: Is noise a kind of pollution, even though you can't see it or touch it? Who should decide how loud a festival or a road can be?
Is music something only humans make, or do whales and birds make music too?
If a flower responds to a bee's hum, do they 'hear'? What does hearing really mean?
Is a quiet street something everyone shares, like clean air?
Would the world be better or worse if we could hear everything a bat or an elephant hears?
When an ambulance passes, its siren sounds higher then lower, but the siren never changes. So which pitch is the real one?

challenge.q: An old story says Pythagoras discovered musical notes by hearing blacksmiths' hammers of different weights. Is it true?
challenge.hint: The story has been told for about 2,000 years, but when people tried it, hammers of different weights do not give notes in the neat way the story says. What is true is that strings whose lengths are in simple ratios (like 2 to 1) sound pleasant together, and the Pythagoreans studied this. Musicians in India and China also worked with these ratios. Ask: why might a story stay popular even when it doesn't work?

challenge.q: People say you can hear the sea when you hold a big shell to your ear. Is it the sea?
challenge.hint: No. The hollow shell resonates with the quiet sounds already around you (and the sound of your own blood flowing) and makes some of them louder, which sounds like waves. Try it with a cupped hand or a steel glass, far from any sea. Ask: how could you test it in a really silent room?

challenge.q: Many people think louder sounds travel faster. Do they?
challenge.hint: No. In the same air, a whisper and a shout travel at the same speed, about 340 metres a second. Loudness changes how far a sound can be heard, not how fast it goes. Pitch doesn't change the speed either, which is why music played far away still sounds in tune.

perspectives.who: Evelyn Glennie (born 1965), a Scottish percussionist who is profoundly deaf
perspectives.view: She lost most of her hearing by the age of 12 but became one of the world's great drummers, often performing barefoot to feel the vibrations through the floor. She says hearing is a kind of touch. Ask: is she hearing the music? What does 'hearing' mean?

perspectives.who: A traffic police officer at a busy junction
perspectives.view: They stand for hours in noise often above 85 dB, breathing traffic fumes. Ask: who chooses the noise of a city, and who has to live inside it?

Scientists have found that some city birds sing louder or at a higher pitch than birds of the same kind in the countryside, so that their songs can be heard over traffic. Ask: how else might noise change the lives of animals that need to hear each other?

perspectives.who: A drum maker who makes mridangams in Chennai or tablas in Varanasi
perspectives.view: The craft of making the black patch on the drum skin is passed from parent to child, by touch and by ear, and takes years to learn. Ask: is this science? What would be lost if no one learned it?

perspectives.who: Al-Jazari (1136–1206), an engineer in the Artuqid kingdom (in today's Turkey)
perspectives.view: In his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices (1206) he described a boat of mechanical musicians for royal parties, and later writers say its drummer's rhythm could be changed by moving pegs on a turning wheel, which is why some historians call it an early programmable machine (others say that goes too far). Ask: if a machine plays music, who is the musician: the machine, its builder, or the one who set the pegs?

story.title: The Bottle That Was Too Low
text: My Appa collects bottles. Not because he likes them, but because that is his work. Every morning he pushes his cart through the lanes of Mylapore calling 'Paper, bottle, iron, plastic!', and every evening he comes home with the cart rattling, and the bottles go in sacks behind our house: green ones, brown ones, clear ones, tall soda bottles and short fat jam jars.
I always thought they sounded like nothing. Then, the week before Music Day at school, I heard Parvathi play the jal tarang.

Parvathi lives three houses down. Her family has a real jal tarang: sixteen white porcelain bowls, each with a different amount of water, arranged in a half-moon on a cloth. She sits cross-legged in the middle and strikes the rims with two thin bamboo sticks, and the notes come out round and clear, like drops of water that have learned to sing.
“I want to play in the Music Day too,” I said.
Parvathi looked at me, and then at the sacks of bottles over our wall. She did not laugh. She said, “Then make one.”

So I did. I took eight bottles, all the same, the tall clear kind from the soda shop. I washed them. I did not tap them, because I did not have proper sticks. Instead I blew across the top of one, the way my cousin had once shown me, and it made a sound like a far-off ship. Hoooo.

I poured water into each bottle and blew, and listened, and poured a little more, and blew again. It took me four evenings. My lips went numb. Amma said I sounded like a train station. But by Thursday I had eight bottles that went up like the steps of a staircase: Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni, Sa.

On Music Day morning I carried them to school in Appa's cart, wrapped in old newspaper so they would not knock together. When I unwrapped them backstage, the hall was already filling up. I could hear the fans whirring and the parents talking and the headmaster tapping the microphone.

I blew a quick scale to check. Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni… and the last Sa was wrong. It was flat, too low, a sad droopy sound that did not belong at the top of the staircase. Some of the water must have spilled in the cart.
My stomach went cold. I had one minute, perhaps two.
Parvathi was next to me, holding her bamboo sticks. She heard it too. “It's too low,” she said quickly. “Take some water out. Quick! When my bowls are too low, I pour a little out.”
I picked up the bottle to tip it. And then I stopped.
Because I remembered the four evenings. Every time I had added water, the note had gone up, not down. More water, higher. Less water, lower. I had learned it with my own sore lips.
“No,” I said. “I have to add water.”
“That will make it lower!” Parvathi whispered. “I know it does. I've been playing since I was five!”
There was no time to argue. I grabbed her water jug, poured in a little, a thumb's width, and blew. Higher. A little more. Higher. There: Sa. Clean and bright at the top of the staircase.
Parvathi stared at me. Then at the bottle. Then at her bowls.
“Tap it,” she said suddenly, and held out a stick.
I tapped the side of my bottle. It made a dull plink. I tapped the bottle next to it, with less water. Its plink was higher.
We looked at each other.
“When you hit it, the glass and the water shake,” Parvathi said slowly. “More water, heavier, slower shaking. Lower.”
“When I blow it,” I said, “it's the air that shakes. The air on top of the water. More water, less air. Shorter air. Faster. Higher.”
“So we're both right,” she said.
“We're both right because we're shaking different things.”

Then the teacher called my name, and I walked out on to the stage with my eight soda bottles, and I could see Appa at the very back of the hall, standing, because he had come straight from his rounds and did not want to sit down in his work clothes. I blew Sa, and the whole hall went quiet.

I played 'Raghupati Raghava', which was the only full song I knew. Halfway through, I heard something behind me: a clear round note, like a drop of water singing. Parvathi had carried her bowls on to the stage and sat down beside me, and she was playing along, her sticks on the rims, my breath across the tops: her water shaking, my air shaking, the same tune.
Afterwards, the headmaster asked us what the instrument was called. Parvathi looked at me.
“It doesn't have a name yet,” I said.

Appa took the bottles home in the cart that evening. But he didn't put them in the sacks. He put them on the shelf by the door, all eight, in a row from Sa to Sa, where the evening light comes through them green and gold.
story.epiphany: Pitch depends on what is vibrating and how fast. When you tap a bottle, the glass and water vibrate: more water means more mass and a lower note. When you blow, the air column above the water vibrates: more water means a shorter column, faster vibration and a higher note. The turn comes when Malar trusts what she learned with her own lips over Parvathi's advice, and then the two children discover together that they were shaking different things.
ask: Why did Parvathi tell Malar to take water out? Was she wrong?
What was really vibrating when Malar blew? When Parvathi tapped?
How did Malar know to add water? Where did her knowledge come from?
Why do you think Appa stood at the back of the hall, and why did he put the bottles on the shelf?
What would you call their new instrument?

ideas.idea: Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle.
ideas.more: No air flows from the drum to your ear. Each particle pushes the next one and swings back. The pass-it-on line and the spoon bell show this.

ideas.idea: Two numbers describe every simple sound: how big the shake is and how fast it is.
ideas.more: Amplitude sets the volume, and frequency sets the pitch. A tabla, a whale and a mosquito all follow these two rules. The drum (harder, louder) and the ruler (shorter, higher) show both.

ideas.idea: Our ears hear only a small slice of all the sounds in the world.
ideas.more: Below 20 hertz, elephants and whales call across great distances. Above 20,000 hertz, bats hunt and thirsty plants click. There are far more sounds around us than we can hear.
One loud speaker fills a whole street, and the people and animals who live there cannot switch it off. Who gets to make noise, and who has to hear it, is a fairness question as well as a science one.

unknowns: Why do humpback whales sing, and why do whole populations change their song together? Scientists have ideas, but nobody knows for sure.
Can plants sense sound and respond to it, and if so, how many do and how? A few exciting studies exist, but the question is still open.

Why do some combinations of notes sound pleasant and others clash? Part of the answer is physics, but part seems to depend on what music people grew up with, and scientists still argue about how much.

books.title: Sound: Loud, Soft, High, and Low
books.author: Natalie M. Rosinsky
books.why: A short, clear picture book on vibration, volume and pitch: a good review before teaching it back.

books.title: Silent Thunder: In the Presence of Elephants
books.author: Katy Payne
books.why: The scientist who discovered elephant infrasound tells how it happened. Read aloud the part about the zoo in Portland.

books.title: Good Vibrations
books.author: Evelyn Glennie
books.why: The deaf percussionist's own story of feeling music through her body. Read a few pages to start a talk about what hearing means.

check.q: How does sound get from a drum to your ear?
check.a: The drum skin vibrates and pushes the air particles next to it, which push the next ones, passing the vibration along until it reaches the eardrum.

check.q: Why does sound travel better through steel than air, and why not at all in a vacuum?
check.a: In steel the particles are packed closely, so they pass on the vibration easily and fast. A vacuum has no particles to pass it on.

check.q: What is the difference between volume and pitch, and what about the vibration controls each?
check.a: Volume is how loud a sound is. It depends on the amplitude, which is how big the vibration is. Pitch is how high or low a sound is. It depends on the frequency, which is how fast the thing vibrates.

check.q: Give three ways to make a string's pitch higher.
check.a: Make it shorter, tighter or thinner.

check.q: Why does adding water make a blown bottle higher but a tapped bottle lower?
check.a: Blowing vibrates the air column, which gets shorter (faster, higher). Tapping vibrates the glass and water, which gets heavier (slower, lower).

check.q: In the muffler test, what were the independent, dependent and control variables?
check.a: Independent: the material. Dependent: the loudness measured. Control: same phone, alarm volume, distance, box and amount of material.

check.q: How did Spallanzani and Jurine find out that bats use their ears to fly in the dark, and why were they doubted?
check.a: Bats who could not see still dodged threads, but bats with plugged ears crashed. People doubted it because no one could hear the bats' calls, which are ultrasound. Griffin detected them in 1938.

check.q: Lightning flashes and thunder comes 12 seconds later. How far away is the storm?
A train horn sounds higher as the train comes towards you and lower as it goes away. Why?
check.a: The Doppler effect: in front of the moving train the sound waves are squashed closer together (higher pitch) and behind it they are stretched out (lower pitch).
